name: Sakalabhuvaneswarar Temple (Ilankoil), Tirumeeyachur
deity: Shiva as Sakalabhuvaneswarar, with the goddess Mekalambikai
tradition: Shaiva — a Paadal Petra Sthalam, sung by Tirunavukkarasar (Appar)
period: Tevaram era; Chola-period Ilankoil within the Meghanathar complex
summary: Within the Meghanathaswamy temple complex at Tirumeeyachur stands a second, distinct Paadal Petra Sthalam — the Ilankoil, the 'young temple' — where Shiva is worshipped as Sakalabhuvaneswarar with the goddess Mekalambikai. Sung by Tirunavukkarasar (Appar), the shrine takes its name from its origin as the balalayam, the temporary temple kept in worship while the main temple was built. Two of the 275 Tevaram shrines thus share a single sacred ground.

sections.history: The Sakalabhuvaneswarar shrine at Tirumeeyachur is a distinct Paadal Petra Sthalam, counted among the 275 Tevaram shrines and sung by Appar. Its name, Ilankoil — the 'young temple' — comes from its origin as the balalayam: the temporary shrine kept in active worship while the great Meghanathar temple was under construction, so that the deity never went unworshipped. It stands to this day on the northern side of the Meghanathaswamy sanctum, within the same complex.
sections.architecture: The Ilankoil follows the Dravidian plan within the northern prakara of the Meghanathar temple. The presiding Sakalabhuvaneswarar faces east, while the goddess Mekalambikai faces south, each in a separate sanctum. Modest in scale beside the main shrine, it is nonetheless a full Paadal Petra temple in its own right, and its placement within a larger complex is part of what makes Tirumeeyachur unusual among Tevaram sites.
sections.legends: The sthala-purana of the shrine connects it to the birth of Vali and Sugreeva, the vanara brothers, and to Surya the sun-god, who is said to have been forgiven here. Another tradition, shared with the larger complex, tells of Shiva granting eggs to the two wives of the sage Kashyapa, from one of which Garuda was born. These stories place the Ilankoil within the rich mythic weave of Tirumeeyachur.
sections.festivals: As part of the Meghanathar complex, the Ilankoil shares in the temple's festival life, with the Shaiva observances of Maha Shivaratri, Pradosham and the Margazhi season, and the great Devi festivals of the main shrine. Devotees completing worship at Tirumeeyachur take in both Paadal Petra shrines, so the Ilankoil receives its share of the complex's steady devotion.
sections.experience: For the pilgrim, the Ilankoil offers the quiet pleasure of discovering a second Tevaram shrine within one temple — a reminder that at Tirumeeyachur the lord was kept in worship even as his larger house was being raised. The darshan of Sakalabhuvaneswarar completes a visit that is as much about the continuity of devotion as about any single sanctum.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: The Ilankoil is within the Meghanathaswamy temple complex at Tirumeeyachur, about 2 km from Peralam near Nannilam in Tiruvarur district; the nearest rail heads are Peralam and Mayiladuthurai.
